29.58: Printed totals | 2,186 vessels | 550,943 empty barrels | 378,347 barrels of herrings | £155,463 11s 0d
29.59: The catch comprised 378,347 barrels packed loosely at sea. The bounty per such barrel averaged 8s 2¼d. Since a barrel packed at sea counts as two-thirds of a fully packed barrel, deduct 126,115⅔ barrels. That leaves 252,231⅓ fully packed barrels, with a bounty of 12s 3¾d on each.
29.60: Export adds a premium of 2s 8d. The government’s cash payment on each barrel then totals 14s 11¾d.
29.61: Add the duty normally credited on the foreign salt allowed for curing each barrel: 1¼ bushels on average at 10s a bushel, or 12s 6d. The bounty then comes to £1 7s 5¾d per barrel.
29.62: With British salt, begin as before at 14s 11¾d. Add duty on two bushels of Scottish salt, the assumed average per barrel, at 1s 6d a bushel, or 3s in all. The bounty totals 17s 11¾d per barrel.
29.63: For herrings landed by the vessels and entered for Scottish consumption, start with the former bounty of 12s 3¾d and deduct the duty of 1s per barrel. This leaves 11s 3¾d.
29.64: Add back the duty of 12s 6d on the foreign salt used per barrel. The premium allowed on a barrel entered for home consumption is thus £1 3s 9¾d.
29.65: For herrings cured with British salt, the same calculation starts from 12s 3¾d a barrel. Deduct the shilling paid when the herrings are entered for home consumption, leaving 11s 3¾d.
29.66: Add the duty of 3s on the two bushels of Scottish salt assumed to be used per barrel, at 1s 6d per bushel. The resulting premium per barrel entered for home consumption is 14s 3¾d.
